title: Word Ladder
description:
# Word Ladder

A **transformation sequence** from word `beginWord` to word `endWord` using a dictionary `wordList` is a sequence of words `beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk` such that:

*   `s1` is in `wordList`.
*   `sk == endWord`.
*   Every adjacent pair of words differs by exactly one letter.
*   Every intermediate word after `beginWord` must be in `wordList`.

Given two words, `beginWord` and `endWord`, and a dictionary `wordList`, return the **number of words** in the shortest transformation sequence from `beginWord` to `endWord`. Return `0` if no such sequence exists.

The answer counts both the starting word and the ending word. For example, `hit -> hot -> dot -> dog -> cog` has length `5`, not `4`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"]
**Output:** 5
**Explanation:** One shortest transformation sequence is "hit" -> "hot" -> "dot" -> "dog" -> "cog", which contains 5 words.

## Example 2:

**Input:** beginWord = "hit", endWord = "cog", wordList = ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log"]
**Output:** 0
**Explanation:** The end word "cog" is not in `wordList`, so no valid transformation sequence can end at it.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= beginWord.length <= 10`
*   `endWord.length == beginWord.length`
*   `1 <= wordList.length <= 5000`
*   `wordList[i].length == beginWord.length`
*   `beginWord`, `endWord`, and `wordList[i]` consist of lowercase English letters.
*   `beginWord != endWord`
*   All words in `wordList` are unique.

solutions.name: Single-Ended Mutation BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Put all dictionary words into a hash set, then run BFS from `beginWord`. For each popped word, try changing every character position to every lowercase letter. If the generated word is in the dictionary, remove it from the dictionary and push it into the next BFS layer.

## Key Insight

Each BFS layer represents one more word in the transformation sequence. The first time BFS generates `endWord`, that layer count is the shortest possible number of words. Removing a word when it is enqueued prevents repeated visits without losing a shorter path.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(N * L * 26)
- Space Complexity: O(N * L)

solutions.name: Bidirectional BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep one frontier growing from `beginWord` and another from `endWord`. On every round, expand the smaller frontier by one-letter mutations. If a generated word appears in the opposite frontier, the two searches have met and the current sequence length is the answer.

## Key Insight

Word Ladder graphs can branch heavily. Bidirectional BFS keeps the shortest-path guarantee of ordinary BFS, but it often explores far fewer words because it searches from both ends and always expands the smaller side.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(N * L * 26)
- Space Complexity: O(N * L)

solutions.name: Wildcard Pattern BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Precompute wildcard buckets. For each word and each position, replace that position with `*`; words sharing the same wildcard pattern are one letter apart. BFS then moves from a word to every word in its wildcard buckets, clearing each bucket after it is used.

## Key Insight

The expensive part of Word Ladder is finding neighbors. Wildcard buckets turn neighbor discovery from trying every possible mutation into a lookup by shared pattern, while BFS still supplies the shortest transformation length.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(N * L^2)
- Space Complexity: O(N * L^2)

solutions.name: Pairwise Graph BFS Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build the implicit Word Ladder graph explicitly. Add `beginWord` as node 0, add every dictionary word once, connect two nodes if their words differ by exactly one letter, and then run ordinary BFS from node 0 to the node holding `endWord`.

## Key Insight

This baseline is slower, but it makes the graph model completely explicit: words are nodes, one-letter changes are edges, and the answer is the shortest unweighted path length counted in nodes. It is useful for understanding why the optimized routes are still BFS problems.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(N^2 * L)
- Space Complexity: O(N^2)
